country.name: France
country.summary: France is the model for the world's wine law and the source of most of the grapes the world grows: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from Bordeaux, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from Burgundy, Syrah and Grenache from the Rhône, Sauvignon Blanc and Chenin Blanc from the Loire, Riesling from Alsace, and the method of Champagne. Its appellation system, the AOC, ranks place rather than grape, so a label usually names a village or a vineyard and leaves the variety unsaid. Three climates shape the map: Atlantic in the west, continental in the north-east, Mediterranean in the south. The exam asks the nine regions of this sheet hardest, with Jura, Savoie, the South West and Corsica as outliers, and above all it asks what the word cru means in each place.
country.overview:
Vines came with the Greeks to Marseille in the sixth century BC and spread with Rome up the Rhône, the Garonne and the Loire. The Church held the great vineyards of Burgundy and Champagne through the Middle Ages, and the Revolution broke them into the small holdings that make Burgundy so complicated today. Phylloxera arrived in the 1860s and forced the whole country onto American rootstocks. The map runs from the Atlantic west, Bordeaux, the Loire mouth and Cognac, through the continental north-east of Champagne, Alsace, Burgundy and Beaujolais, to the Mediterranean south of the Rhône, Provence and Languedoc-Roussillon, with Jura and Savoie against the Alps, the South West behind Bordeaux and Corsica offshore.

The appellation system grew out of the fraud and overproduction that followed phylloxera. Châteauneuf-du-Pape wrote the first modern rules for itself in 1923, the national appellation committee, today’s INAO, was founded by the decree-law of 1935 and the AOC decrees followed. Under the EU scheme of 2009 the AOC is also an AOP, Vin de Pays became IGP and Vin de Table became Vin de France. Each AOC fixes the area, the grapes, the yields, the minimum ripeness and the methods. Above that floor every region ranks differently: Bordeaux ranks estates in the growths of 1855, Burgundy and Alsace rank vineyards, Champagne ranks villages, Beaujolais and the Rhône name their crus as separate appellations, and Saint-Émilion rewrites its list about every ten years. Many French appellations emphasise place rather than grape. Alsace is particularly associated with varietal labelling, but IGP, Vin de France and other permitted appellation labels can also name grapes.

The exam leans on grape-to-place matching, on the meaning of cru, on Champagne's dosage ladder and method, Burgundy's four-tier pyramid, the 1855 First Growths, the northern and southern Rhône, the Loire's four districts and Alsace's noble grapes and two late-harvest categories. It expects the label words: mis en bouteille au château or au domaine, négociant, vieilles vignes, supérieur, sec and demi-sec, brut and extra dry. It also expects the other methods France gave the world: the eight Crémant appellations, Vin Doux Naturel by mutage, Vin de Liqueur, and the Jura's Vin Jaune under its veil of yeast.
ladder: The base tier, once Vin de Table: no place smaller than France, though grape and vintage may be shown.
Indication Géographique Protégée, since 2009: broader areas and looser rules, the grape usually on the label (Pays d'Oc, Val de Loire).
Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée, the law of 1935: delimited area, permitted grapes, maximum yields, minimum ripeness, methods; nearly all the wine the exam asks.
Bordeaux, Bourgogne, Côtes du Rhône, Alsace, Touraine: the whole region's name.
Pauillac, Meursault, Gigondas, Vouvray, Sancerre: a commune or a small district, the grape implied.

Ranked ground, estate or village depending on the region: Grand Cru and Premier Cru in Burgundy, Chablis, Alsace and Champagne; Cru Classé in Bordeaux; the ten crus of Beaujolais and the crus of the Rhône as appellations of their own.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted grape in France, the heart of Right Bank Bordeaux and of the Languedoc's everyday reds.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Left Bank Bordeaux's lead, blended with Merlot and Cabernet Franc; cassis, cedar and long life.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Burgundy's red, Champagne's body, Sancerre's red and Alsace's one black grape.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Burgundy's white from Chablis to the Mâconnais and the backbone of Champagne.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Syrah here: the northern Rhône's only black grape and the spice in southern blends.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Grenache: the southern Rhône, Provence rosé, Languedoc-Roussillon and the Vins Doux Naturels.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, Touraine, and the aromatic half of dry white Bordeaux.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: The Loire's great white in every style from bone dry to botrytised to sparkling.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Alsace's finest grape, dry by default, almost nowhere else in France.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: Beaujolais and its ten crus, with light reds across the Loire.

grapes.name: Melon de Bourgogne
grapes.styles: Muscadet at the Loire's mouth, bone dry and saline.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Bordeaux's third red and the Loire's lead red at Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: The weight in white Bordeaux and the botrytis grape of Sauternes.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre / Monastrell
grapes.styles: Mourvèdre: Bandol's lead and the tannin in southern Rhône blends.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Condrieu's perfumed white and a co-ferment in Côte-Rôtie.

grapes.name: Ugni Blanc
grapes.styles: The most planted white grape of France, distilled for Cognac and Armagnac and rarely seen on a wine list.

exam: Know the three tiers, Vin de France, IGP and AOC, and the 1935 law behind the AOC.
Say what cru means in each region: estate in Bordeaux, vineyard in Burgundy and Alsace, village in Champagne, an appellation of its own in Beaujolais and the Rhône.
Match grape to region for the classics: many appellation labels emphasise place. Alsace is known for varietal labelling, but it is not the only French region to name grapes.
Hold the sweetness words, still and sparkling, and know that Extra Dry sits sweeter than Brut.
Know the eight Crémants, the Vins Doux Naturels and Vin Jaune as the country's other methods.
Expect the Loire, Rhône and Burgundy ladders from regional name to village to cru.
traps: Grand Cru is the top in Burgundy, Chablis, Alsace and Champagne, but in Saint-Émilion plain Grand Cru is a broad lower tier.
Supérieur means a little more alcohol, not better wine.
Vieilles vignes has no legal minimum age.
Pomerol has no classification at all.
A Burgundy Grand Cru label shows the vineyard alone; a Champagne Grand Cru names a village; a Bordeaux Grand Cru Classé names an estate.
Crémant is never Champagne, and méthode champenoise is reserved to Champagne: every other bottle-fermented French wine says méthode traditionnelle.
Alsace commonly names grapes, but other French appellations, IGP and Vin de France may also carry varietal labels.

cards.f: France's three tiers of wine law
cards.b: Vin de France (no place smaller than the country), IGP (Vin de Pays, broader areas, grape on the label), AOC/AOP (delimited area, grapes, yields, methods; the law of 1935).

cards.f: What cru means, region by region
cards.b: Bordeaux: a classified estate. Burgundy, Chablis, Alsace: a vineyard. Champagne: a village. Beaujolais and the Rhône: a named appellation of its own.

cards.f: Grape to region, the classics
cards.b: Bordeaux: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. Burgundy: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Beaujolais: Gamay. Rhône: Syrah north, Grenache south. Loire: Chenin, Sauvignon, Melon, Cabernet Franc. Alsace: Riesling. Champagne: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Meunier.

cards.f: The eight Crémant appellations
cards.b: Alsace, Bourgogne, Loire, Limoux, Jura, Die, Bordeaux, Savoie: traditional-method sparkling wines outside Champagne.

cards.f: Still-wine sweetness words in French
cards.b: Sec (dry), demi-sec (off-dry), moelleux (sweet), doux or liquoreux (very sweet).

cards.f: Three climates of France and their regions
cards.b: Atlantic: Bordeaux, the Loire mouth, the South West. Continental: Champagne, Alsace, Burgundy, Beaujolais, the northern Rhône, the upper Loire. Mediterranean: southern Rhône, Provence, Languedoc-Roussillon, Corsica.

cards.f: Vin Doux Naturel: method and names
cards.b: Fermentation stopped by adding grape spirit (mutage), keeping sugar: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, Rasteau, Banyuls, Maury, Rivesaltes, Muscat de Frontignan.

cards.f: Estate words on a French label
cards.b: Château (Bordeaux), Domaine (Burgundy), Clos (walled vineyard), Mas (southern farm), Monopole (one owner); mis en bouteille au château or au domaine means estate bottled.

cards.f: Vin Jaune in one card
cards.b: Jura, Savagnin, aged under a yeast veil without topping up for at least six years and three months, bottled in the 62 cl clavelin; Château-Chalon is its own appellation.

questions.q: Which tier of French wine law sits between Vin de France and AOC?
questions.exp: IGP, Indication Géographique Protégée, replaced Vin de Pays in 2009 as the middle tier; it covers broader areas with looser rules and usually names the grape.

questions.q: In which year did the decree-law creating the Appellation d’Origine Contrôlée pass?
questions.exp: The decree-law of 1935 created the Appellation d’Origine Contrôlée and the national appellation committee that became the INAO, after the fraud that followed phylloxera; Châteauneuf-du-Pape’s own rules of 1923 were the model.

questions.q: In which region does Grand Cru rank a whole village rather than a vineyard or an estate?
questions.exp: Champagne ranks communes: seventeen Grand Cru villages. Burgundy and Alsace rank vineyards, and Bordeaux ranks estates as Crus Classés.

questions.q: Which region of France labels its wines by grape variety as a rule?
questions.exp: Alsace is especially associated with grape names on labels. This is a regional convention, not a French monopoly: other appellations, IGP and Vin de France may also name varieties. Pinot Blanc in Alsace can include Auxerrois.

questions.q: What does mis en bouteille au château mean on a Bordeaux label?
questions.exp: The wine was bottled at the property that grew it; the Burgundy equivalent is mis en bouteille au domaine, and à la propriété serves anywhere.

questions.q: Which French region ranks its estates in a classification dating from 1855?
questions.exp: The 1855 classification ranked the Médoc's châteaux, with Haut-Brion from the Graves, in five growths and Sauternes separately, on the prices of the day; it is the model of estate ranking.

questions.q: Which word on a French label means that the vineyard has a single owner?
questions.exp: Monopole marks a vineyard held entirely by one producer, rare in Burgundy where inheritance split most sites; La Tâche, Clos de Tart and Coulée de Serrant are examples.

questions.q: Which French wine category is made by adding grape spirit during fermentation so that the grape's own sugar remains?
questions.exp: Vin Doux Naturel stops fermentation by mutage, keeping grape sugar: Banyuls, Maury, Rivesaltes, Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise. Vin de Liqueur fortifies unfermented must; Vin Jaune and Vin de Paille are unfortified Jura wines.

regions.name: Champagne
regions.summary: Champagne is the benchmark sparkling wine, grown at the cold northern edge of French viticulture around Reims and Épernay. Three grapes carry nearly the whole vineyard: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier. The wine is made by the traditional method, a second fermentation in the bottle it is sold in, followed by months or years on the lees. Chalk beneath the slopes stores water and gives the cellars. Cru rank attaches to whole villages, seventeen of them Grand Cru. A server needs the method in order, the sweetness ladder with Extra Dry sweeter than Brut, the four districts and their grapes, and the ageing minimums of fifteen months for non-vintage and three years for vintage.

terroir.climate: Cool conditions with both oceanic and continental influences help grapes retain acidity. Spring frost, hail and wet-season disease pressure are significant challenges; warm or dry seasons bring different decisions about ripeness and harvest timing. The aim is a balanced base wine rather than deliberately unripe fruit. Voltis is an adaptation variety with disease-resistance benefits and specific controls, not simply a replacement for the established grapes.
terroir.soils: Chalk is important, especially in the Côte des Blancs, Côte de Sézanne and Vitryat: its porosity supports both drainage and water storage. Clay, marl, sand and hard limestone also occur. The Côte des Bar includes Jurassic limestone and marl. Ground varies within every district; a map-level soil description does not establish a parcel’s geology or explain a flavour on its own.
terroir.topography: Low, gentle slopes rather than mountains. The Montagne de Reims is a wooded plateau whose vine-clad flanks face north, east and south; the Côte des Blancs is a single east-facing chalk escarpment south of Épernay; the Marne cuts a valley between them with vines on both banks. The Côte des Bar lies about 100 kilometres south-east, nearer Chablis than Reims.
terroir.water: The Marne runs through the heart of the region, tempering the frost-prone valley slopes and naming the central district; the Aube and the Seine mark the southern vineyards. The sea is far away, felt only as mild, damp westerly air.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Especially associated with the Côte des Blancs; often brings freshness, citrus and floral notes. It is the usual grape of Blanc de Blancs, although that term permits other white varieties.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Body, red fruit and structure from the Montagne de Reims and the Côte des Bar; Blanc de Noirs and most rosé lean on it.

grapes.name: Meunier
grapes.styles: Later budburst helps Meunier in frost-prone sites. It is particularly important in the western Marne Valley and often adds fruit and roundness; its name alone does not determine how long a wine will age.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: One of the less common principal varieties, alongside Pinot Gris, Arbane, Petit Meslier and Chardonnay rose. Together with Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, these make eight principal varieties under the July 2025 rules. Voltis has separate conditional adaptation status.

wines.note: The house style and most of what is sold: a blend across grapes, villages and years, dry under 12 grams of sugar, apple, citrus and brioche. Serve at 8 to 10 degrees with oysters, fried food or a whole meal.
From a single harvest year, with release at least 36 months after tirage. The vintage describes the harvest, not a guaranteed level of richness, toastiness or quality.

White-grape Champagne, usually Chardonnay but not necessarily Chardonnay alone. Citrus, floral and developed flavours depend on site, blend and ageing; select a bottle for the dish rather than relying on the category alone.
A white wine from black grapes only, Pinot Noir or Meunier: broader, red-fruited and vinous, for roast chicken or duck.
Usually made by adding a little still red to the blend, legal here and almost nowhere else in France, sometimes by saignée; dry berry fruit for salmon and lamb.
A house's top bottling, often vintage and long aged: Dom Pérignon, Cristal, Comtes de Champagne, Grande Cuvée. The term has no legal definition.
32 to 50 grams of sugar: gently sweet, for fruit desserts, wedding cake and pastry.
Still wine from the Champagne vineyard in all three colours; the light red of Bouzy or Aÿ is the one a list carries.
A still Pinot Noir rosé from one Aube commune, made only in ripe years, deeper than most pink wine.

made.viticulture: Vineyard work includes pruning, shoot positioning, canopy management and monitoring fruit health and ripeness. Chablis, Cordon de Royat, Guyot and Vallée de la Marne are recognised pruning systems; the last is limited to Meunier. Harvest timing varies by commune and grape. Picking is by hand so whole bunches can arrive at the press. Spring frost, hail, rain and disease pressure affect sites and years differently; later-budding Meunier is not immune to damage. Reserve stocks help manage harvest variation. Under the July 2025 specification, Voltis requires an adaptation agreement, normally occupies no more than 5 per cent of the holding and may make up no more than 10 per cent of a blend. Qualifying plantings close to inhabited sites are excluded from the holding-area calculation. Chardonnay rose is a principal variety, not part of that Voltis category.
made.winemaking: Pressing is gentle and fractionated: 4,000 kilograms of grapes yield at most 2,550 litres, the first 2,050 the cuvée and the last 500 the taille. The juice ferments to a dry, sharp still wine, the vin clair, usually in steel, sometimes in oak, and most houses allow malolactic conversion. In spring the winemaker blends across villages, grapes and reserve wines from earlier years for a non-vintage, or from one year alone for a vintage. The blend goes into bottle with the liqueur de tirage, sugar and yeast, and a second fermentation builds about six atmospheres of pressure. The wine then rests on its lees, at least twelve months for non-vintage, while the dead yeast breaks down and gives the bready, biscuit register. Riddling, remuage, walks the sediment into the neck, by hand on pupitres or by machine in gyropalettes; the neck is frozen and the plug expelled at disgorgement; the bottle is topped up with the liqueur d'expédition, whose sugar fixes the sweetness level; then cork, wire cage and label. Fifteen months must pass between tirage and release for non-vintage, thirty-six for vintage.

law.classification: One appellation, Champagne, covers the whole sparkling vineyard, with Coteaux Champenois for still wine and Rosé des Riceys for one still rosé. Within it the ranking attaches to villages, not vineyards: seventeen communes hold Grand Cru and forty-two hold Premier Cru, a legacy of the échelle des crus, the percentage scale that once set grape prices and no longer fixes any price at all. A label may claim Grand Cru only when every grape came from Grand Cru villages. The producer's status appears as two small letters: NM for a house that buys grapes, RM for a grower who makes wine from its own fruit, CM for a cooperative, RC for a grower selling cooperative-made wine, SR for a family company, ND for a merchant distributor and MA for a buyer's own brand. Sweetness terms are defined by residual sugar, and the ageing minimums run from tirage.
tiers: Champagne AOC
The whole sparkling appellation; the name alone is the guarantee, and the word Champagne is reserved to it in law.
Grand Cru
Seventeen villages rated at the full 100 per cent on the old scale; the label may say Grand Cru only when all the fruit is from them.
Premier Cru
Forty-two villages rated 90 to 99 per cent; the same all-or-nothing rule applies.
Autres crus
The remaining villages, once rated 80 to 89 per cent; most non-vintage blends draw on them.
Coteaux Champenois
Still red, white or rosé from the Champagne vineyard; Bouzy and Aÿ reds are the best known.
Rosé des Riceys
A still rosé of Pinot Noir from the commune of Les Riceys in the Aube, declared only in ripe years.

places.name: Montagne de Reims
places.note: The wooded plateau south of Reims, ringed by villages that face north and east yet rank at the top for Pinot Noir: structure and body for the blend.

places.name: Reims
places.note: The cathedral city, seat of Krug, Roederer, Taittinger, Veuve Clicquot, Ruinart and Pommery, with the crayères beneath it.

places.name: Verzenay
places.note: North-facing Grand Cru with a landmark windmill; firm, long-lived Pinot Noir despite the aspect.

places.name: Verzy
places.note: Grand Cru beside Verzenay, also facing north, Pinot Noir with Chardonnay rising.

places.name: Bouzy
places.note: Grand Cru on the warm southern flank: Pinot Noir for blends and the best-known red Coteaux Champenois.

places.name: Ambonnay
places.note: Grand Cru next to Bouzy, Pinot Noir of depth and the home of celebrated growers.

places.name: Mailly-Champagne, Sillery, Beaumont-sur-Vesle, Puisieulx, Louvois
places.note: The Montagne's other five Grand Cru villages; with Verzenay, Verzy, Bouzy and Ambonnay it holds nine of the seventeen.

places.name: Chigny-les-Roses and Rilly-la-Montagne
places.note: Premier Cru villages on the northern slope, Meunier and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Vallée de la Marne
places.note: The river valley west of Épernay includes clay, marl and sandy ground. Meunier is prominent farther west; the eastern valley around Aÿ is strongly associated with Pinot Noir. These are broad tendencies, not exclusive planting rules.

places.name: Épernay
places.note: The trade town on the Marne, home of Moët & Chandon, Pol Roger and Perrier-Jouët and of the Avenue de Champagne.

places.name: Aÿ
places.note: Grand Cru Pinot Noir village on the Grande Vallée, seat of Bollinger and Deutz and the origin of Gosset.

places.name: Mareuil-sur-Aÿ
places.note: Premier Cru next to Aÿ, home of Billecart-Salmon and of Clos des Goisses, a steep walled single vineyard.

places.name: Tours-sur-Marne
places.note: At the eastern end of the Grande Vallée, rated Grand Cru for Pinot Noir; the seat of Laurent-Perrier.

places.name: Hautvillers, Dizy, Cumières and Tauxières
places.note: Premier Cru villages of the Grande Vallée; Hautvillers holds the abbey where Dom Pérignon was cellarer around 1700.

places.name: Pierry
places.note: Premier Cru grower village just south of Épernay, Meunier and Chardonnay.

places.name: Romery
places.note: A small grower village near Hautvillers in the valley's Meunier country.

places.name: Côte des Blancs
places.note: Chalk slopes south of Épernay, strongly associated with Chardonnay and Blanc de Blancs. Exposure and producer decisions still vary; the district name does not guarantee a wine’s lifespan.

places.name: Chouilly
places.note: Northernmost Grand Cru of the Côte, rated 100 for Chardonnay alone.

places.name: Cramant
places.note: Grand Cru on pure chalk, Chardonnay of creamy weight.

places.name: Avize
places.note: Grand Cru at the heart of the Côte, cradle of the grower movement.

places.name: Oger and Oiry
places.note: Grand Cru villages associated with Chardonnay: Oger lies south of Avize towards Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, while Oiry lies to the north-east of Avize.

places.name: Le Mesnil-sur-Oger
places.note: Grand Cru village associated with Chardonnay, including Salon and Krug’s Clos du Mesnil. The individual wine’s style and ageing depend on the producer, cuvée and harvest.

places.name: Vertus
places.note: Premier Cru at the southern end, the Côte's largest village, mostly Chardonnay.

places.name: Côte de Sézanne
places.note: A southern continuation of the Côte des Blancs on the same chalk, Chardonnay that ripens rounder and earlier.

places.name: Côte des Bar
places.note: The Aube's vineyard a hundred kilometres south-east, on Kimmeridgian marl near Chablis: Pinot Noir country, excluded in 1908 and restored in 1927, now a lively grower scene.

places.name: Urville
places.note: Village on the Bar-sur-Aube side, seat of Drappier, a Pinot Noir house.

places.name: Les Riceys
places.note: Three villages in one commune with their own still rosé appellation, Rosé des Riceys.

places.name: Bar-sur-Aube, Bar-sur-Seine and Celles-sur-Ource
places.note: The two towns that name the Côte and a grower village on the Seine side.

places.name: Montgueux
places.note: A lone Chardonnay hill west of Troyes, rich and exotic for the region.

places.name: Massif de Saint-Thierry
places.note: Sandy slopes north-west of Reims, Meunier and Pinot Noir; Merfy is its best-known grower village.

places.name: Vitryat
places.note: A Chardonnay outpost near Vitry-le-François, east of the main districts, on chalk.

producers.name: Krug
producers.why: Reims house founded in 1843; Grande Cuvée is a multi-vintage blend fermented in small old oak and numbered by edition.

producers.name: Bollinger
producers.why: Aÿ house of 1829, Pinot Noir-led and partly fermented in old oak; Special Cuvée NV and La Grande Année vintage.

producers.name: Louis Roederer
producers.why: Reims house of 1776 with unusually large estate vineyards; Cristal, first made for the Russian court in 1876, is its prestige cuvée in clear glass.

producers.name: Moët & Chandon
producers.why: Épernay, 1743, the largest house; Dom Pérignon is its vintage prestige cuvée.

producers.name: Veuve Clicquot
producers.why: Reims, 1772; the widow Clicquot's cellar is credited with riddling in the 1810s; Yellow Label NV is Pinot Noir-led.

producers.name: Pol Roger
producers.why: Épernay family house of 1849; Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill is the prestige wine.

producers.name: Taittinger
producers.why: Reims house with a Chardonnay-leaning style; Comtes de Champagne is a Blanc de Blancs prestige cuvée.

producers.name: Billecart-Salmon
producers.why: Mareuil-sur-Aÿ family house of 1818, known for cool fermentation, finesse and a famous rosé.

producers.name: Ruinart
producers.why: The oldest Champagne house, 1729, in Reims; Chardonnay-led, its crayères open to visitors.

producers.name: Salon
producers.why: One wine only: a Blanc de Blancs from Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, one vintage, declared a few times a decade.

producers.name: Charles Heidsieck
producers.why: Reims house of 1851 whose non-vintage carries an unusually high share of reserve wine.

producers.name: Piper-Heidsieck
producers.why: Reims house of 1785; a fruit-forward Brut NV, and the prestige cuvée Rare began here before it was given a house name of its own.

producers.name: Laurent-Perrier
producers.why: Tours-sur-Marne; Chardonnay-led house style, a non-vintage rosé made by saignée, and Grand Siècle.

producers.name: Perrier-Jouët

exam: Say the traditional method in order: base wine, blending, tirage, second fermentation, lees ageing, riddling, disgorgement, dosage, cork.
Know the dosage ladder in grams per litre, and that Extra Dry sits sweeter than Brut.
Associate Chardonnay with the Côte des Blancs, Pinot Noir with the Montagne de Reims and Côte des Bar, and Meunier with the western Marne Valley; recognise exceptions.
Hold the ageing minimums: 15 months for non-vintage with 12 on the lees, 36 months for vintage, both counted from tirage.
Know that cru rank attaches to villages: 17 Grand Cru and 42 Premier Cru.
Match the prestige cuvées to their houses and the label codes NM, RM and CM to what they mean.
Be ready for bottle sizes: magnum 1.5 litres, Jeroboam 3, Methuselah 6, Nebuchadnezzar 15.
Know the three dominant grapes, the eight principal varieties authorised in July 2025, and the separate conditions attached to Voltis.
traps: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut; Brut Nature is the driest term, not Extra Brut.
Meunier is a major legal grape, and the rules name it plainly, so a server may say Meunier without Pinot.
Rosé by blending red into white is legal in Champagne and almost nowhere else in AOC France.
Grand Cru ranks a whole village, not a vineyard; a Clos on a Champagne label is a walled site, not a rank.
Crémant is traditional-method sparkling wine from elsewhere in France; it may never be called Champagne.
Vintage Champagne needs three years by law, but the great houses hold it far longer; the minimum is not the custom.
The Côte des Bar is in the Aube, not the Marne, and it lies closer to Chablis than to Reims.
A prestige cuvée is a house's own term with no legal definition.

cards.f: Champagne's three main grapes, and the district each leads
cards.b: Chardonnay is especially associated with the Côte des Blancs; Pinot Noir with the Montagne de Reims and Côte des Bar; Meunier with the western Marne Valley. The eastern valley around Aÿ has substantial Pinot Noir.

cards.f: Dosage ladder, driest to sweetest, in grams per litre
cards.b: Brut Nature under 3, with no sugar added after secondary fermentation; Extra Brut 0 to 6; Brut under 12; Extra Dry 12 to 17; Sec 17 to 32; Demi-Sec 32 to 50; Doux over 50 grams per litre.

cards.f: Minimum ageing for non-vintage and vintage Champagne
cards.b: Non-vintage: 15 months from tirage, 12 of them on the lees. Vintage: 36 months from tirage.

cards.f: The traditional method in order
cards.b: Base wine, assemblage, tirage, second fermentation in bottle, lees ageing, riddling (remuage), disgorgement (dégorgement), dosage (liqueur d'expédition), cork and cage.

cards.f: Grand Cru and Premier Cru in Champagne: what is ranked, and how many
cards.b: Whole villages, not vineyards: 17 Grand Cru and 42 Premier Cru communes.

cards.f: Blanc de Blancs versus Blanc de Noirs
cards.b: Blanc de Blancs: white grapes, usually Chardonnay but not necessarily Chardonnay alone. Blanc de Noirs: black grapes, Pinot Noir, Meunier or both, pressed with limited extraction from their skins.

cards.f: Label codes NM, RM, CM
cards.b: NM négociant-manipulant, a house buying grapes; RM récoltant-manipulant, a grower using its own fruit; CM coopérative de manipulation.

cards.f: Prestige cuvées and their houses
cards.b: Dom Pérignon (Moët & Chandon), Cristal (Louis Roederer), Comtes de Champagne (Taittinger), Sir Winston Churchill (Pol Roger), Grande Cuvée (Krug), Belle Epoque (Perrier-Jouët).

cards.f: Champagne bottle sizes, 1.5 litres and up
cards.b: Magnum 1.5 L, Jeroboam 3 L, Rehoboam 4.5 L, Methuselah 6 L, Salmanazar 9 L, Balthazar 12 L, Nebuchadnezzar 15 L.

cards.f: The pressing fractions from 4,000 kilograms
cards.b: 2,550 litres in all: the cuvée is the first 2,050 litres, the taille the last 500.

questions.q: Which Champagne district is planted mainly to Meunier?
questions.exp: Meunier is particularly important in the western Marne Valley, and later budburst can help reduce frost exposure. The eastern valley around Aÿ has substantial Pinot Noir. The other district-to-grape associations are broad tendencies, not exclusive planting rules.

questions.q: Which Champagne sweetness term is the next step sweeter than Brut?
questions.exp: Extra Dry is 12 to 17 grams per litre, the step above Brut's ceiling of 12, so it is sweeter than Brut despite its name. Sec (17 to 32) and Demi-Sec (32 to 50) are sweeter still; Extra Brut (0 to 6) is drier.

questions.q: What is the minimum ageing for a non-vintage Champagne, counted from tirage?
questions.exp: Fifteen months in all, of which twelve must be on the lees. Thirty-six months is the vintage minimum, and most houses exceed both.

questions.q: Grand Cru on a Champagne label attaches to what kind of place?
questions.exp: Champagne ranks entire communes on the old échelle des crus; seventeen hold Grand Cru. Burgundy ranks vineyards and Bordeaux ranks estates.

questions.q: Which Champagne district lies in the Aube, nearer to Chablis than to Reims?
questions.exp: The Côte des Bar sits a hundred kilometres south-east of Épernay on Kimmeridgian marl; it was excluded in 1908 and restored to the appellation in 1927.

questions.q: Which house makes the prestige cuvée Cristal?
questions.exp: Cristal is Roederer's prestige cuvée, first made in 1876 for the Russian court and bottled in clear glass. Moët makes Dom Pérignon, Taittinger Comtes de Champagne and Pol Roger Sir Winston Churchill.

questions.q: Name the step in which the frozen plug of sediment is expelled from the bottle.
questions.exp: After riddling has gathered the lees in the neck, the neck is frozen and the cap removed so that pressure ejects the plug; dosage and corking follow.

questions.q: How many villages hold Grand Cru rank in Champagne?
questions.exp: Seventeen communes are Grand Cru and forty-two are Premier Cru. Seven is the count of Chablis Grand Cru climats and fifty-one the count of Alsace Grand Crus.

regions.name: Alsace
regions.summary: Alsace runs along the eastern foothills of the Vosges, from Strasbourg towards Colmar and Thann. Its labels commonly name grapes, though this is not unique in France. Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat are the four noble varieties, central to fifty-one Grand Cru sites with written exceptions. White styles range from dry to sweet: check the label rather than guessing. Since the 2021 vintage, AOC Alsace whites outside Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles must indicate sweetness. Pinot Blanc may include Auxerrois. Crémant d'Alsace is traditional-method sparkling wine; Pinot Noir makes red and rosé. Vineyard soils, slopes and producer choices give the region considerable stylistic variety.

terroir.climate: Semi-continental, dry and sunny: the Vosges force Atlantic weather to drop its rain on the western side, so Colmar is among the driest towns in France at roughly 500 to 600 millimetres a year. Long, warm, dry autumns let aromatic grapes hang late, which is why the sweet categories are possible and rot is rare. Winters are cold and spring frost threatens the plain more than the slopes.
terroir.soils: A mosaic unlike any other French region: the Rhine rift shattered the ground, so granite, gneiss, schist, volcanic rock, sandstone, limestone, marl and clay all appear within a few kilometres. Granite crus such as Schlossberg and Brand sit at the mouths of valleys; the Rangen above Thann is volcanic; Kastelberg is schist; most of the lower foothills are limestone and marl, the richest ground for Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris.
terroir.topography: The vineyards sit on the foothill shelf between the forested Vosges and the flat Rhine plain, mostly at 200 to 400 metres, on slopes facing east and south-east into the morning sun. The steepest Grand Cru sites climb above the villages; the plain below carries the everyday wines. Colmar and Rouffach lie in the driest pocket behind the highest peaks.
terroir.water: The Rhine flows north along the German border some 20 kilometres east of the vines and the Ill runs parallel through the plain; neither touches the vineyard directly, and the climate owes more to the mountains than to the rivers.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The region's finest, fermented dry in the classic style: lime, stone, steel and a long life, from granite and sandstone above all.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Deep gold, low in acid, heady with lychee, rose and ginger; richest on marl and limestone, and the natural Vendanges Tardives grape.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Pinot Gris here, once sold as Tokay d'Alsace: broad, smoky, orchard-fruited and often carrying a little sugar.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains and Muscat Ottonel: smells of the grape itself and finishes dry; the asparagus wine.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: With Auxerrois, the everyday white and the backbone of Crémant d'Alsace.

grapes.name: Auxerrois
grapes.styles: Softer and lower in acid than Pinot Blanc, with which it is usually blended and often labelled.

grapes.name: Silvaner
grapes.styles: Spelt Sylvaner here: light, earthy and dry, admitted to one Grand Cru, Zotzenberg.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The one black grape, once pale and light, now riper; admitted to Grand Cru at Hengst and Kirchberg de Barr from the 2022 vintage and at Vorbourg from 2024.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Permitted in Crémant d'Alsace only, never in a still Alsace white.

wines.note: Dry, taut, citrus and wet stone, growing to petrol and honey with age; the match for choucroute, trout and smoked fish.
Opulent, spiced and often off-dry: Munster cheese, foie gras, Thai and Creole spice.
Full, smoky, with pear and honey, dry to off-dry; roast pork, mushrooms and richer poultry.
Dry and grapey, served young and cold with asparagus or as an aperitif.
Traditional-method sparkling, mostly Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois, the rosé from Pinot Noir alone; the second largest sparkling appellation in France after Champagne.
Late harvest of a noble grape at a set ripeness, rich and often but not always sweet.
Botrytised berries picked in passes: always sweet, rare and long-lived, for foie gras or on its own.
Light to medium red-cherry Pinot served cool; now Grand Cru at Hengst, Kirchberg de Barr and Vorbourg.
The blends: Edelzwicker any mix of permitted whites with no vintage needed; Gentil at least half noble grapes, each vinified apart.

made.viticulture: Vines are trained high on wires, higher than in most of France, to keep the fruit above the cold air that pools on the plain and to shade heavy bunches in a sunny year. Grand Cru sites are held to lower yields than plain Alsace and must carry a vintage; many growers in the Haut-Rhin farm organically or biodynamically, a movement that took root here early. Harvest runs long, from early September for the Crémant base through October for the noble grapes, with Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles picked last, by hand, declared in advance and checked by the authorities. Minimum must weights for those two categories are set by grape: 235 grams of sugar per litre for Riesling and Muscat Vendanges Tardives and 257 for Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer, rising to 276 and 306 for Sélection de Grains Nobles, with chaptalisation forbidden for both. Hail and spring frost are the old hazards; drought on the thin granite soils is the newer one.
made.winemaking: The classic cellar is simple and reductive: whole-bunch pressing, a cool fermentation in stainless steel or in the large old oval casks, the foudres, that line Alsace cellars and give no oak flavour, then early bottling to keep the aromatics. Malolactic conversion is usually avoided in Riesling and the aromatic grapes to hold acidity. The argument of the last thirty years has been sweetness: some houses ferment everything dry, others stop fermentation and leave sugar in Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, so since the 2021 vintage AOC Alsace whites outside the two late-harvest categories must declare their level on the label, as sec, demi-sec, moelleux or doux or on a printed scale. Crémant d'Alsace is made by the traditional method with a second fermentation in bottle, at least nine months on the lees and twelve months from tirage before sale. Riesling must be entirely Riesling, but Pinot Blanc may include Auxerrois; do not apply one blanket varietal rule. The appellation requires regional bottling, with the flûte prescribed for its still whites.

law.classification: Three appellations covered the region until 2011, when each Grand Cru became an appellation of its own and the count rose to fifty-three: AOC Alsace (1962), the fifty-one Alsace Grand Cru appellations (a tier created in 1975 with Schlossberg as its first site, completed by Kaefferkopf in 2007) and Crémant d'Alsace (1976). Below Grand Cru the 2011 rules also recognised communal denominations such as Côte de Rouffach or Ottrott and named lieux-dits, each with lower yields and higher ripeness than plain Alsace. Grand Cru wine must come from one of the four noble grapes, with exceptions written into a site's own rules: Sylvaner at Zotzenberg, blends at Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf, and Pinot Noir at Hengst and Kirchberg de Barr from the 2022 vintage and Vorbourg from 2024. Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles, defined in 1984, are label mentions limited to the noble four. A Premier Cru tier proposed by the growers was still before the appellation authorities when this was written.

places.name: Bas-Rhin
places.note: The northern department around Strasbourg: fewer Grand Crus, lighter soils, Sylvaner and Pinot Blanc country, and the Klevener of Heiligenstein.

places.name: Barr
places.note: Town of the Kirchberg de Barr, one of the two Grand Crus opened to Pinot Noir from the 2022 vintage.

places.name: Mittelbergheim
places.note: Village of Zotzenberg, the Grand Cru that admits Sylvaner under a 2005 amendment.

places.name: Andlau
places.note: Home of Kastelberg on dark schist, Riesling of unusual longevity, with Wiebelsberg and Moenchberg nearby.

places.name: Epfig and Nothalten
places.note: Villages of the Muenchberg Grand Cru and a leading Bas-Rhin estate.

places.name: Marlenheim
places.note: The northernmost Grand Cru, Steinklotz, near the Strasbourg end of the wine road.

places.name: Heiligenstein
places.note: Five communes here alone may label Klevener de Heiligenstein, the pink-skinned Savagnin Rose.

places.name: Haut-Rhin
places.note: The southern department around Colmar: the driest climate, the richest soils and most of the fifty-one Grand Crus.

places.name: Colmar
places.note: Capital of the wine trade and among the driest towns in France, in the lee of the highest Vosges.

places.name: Ribeauvillé
places.note: Town of three Grand Crus, Geisberg, Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé and Osterberg, and of the region's great dry-Riesling house.

places.name: Hunawihr
places.note: Village of the Rosacker Grand Cru, within which the walled Clos Sainte Hune grows the most famous Riesling in Alsace.

places.name: Riquewihr
places.note: Walled medieval town with the Schoenenbourg and Sporen Grand Crus, marl and gypsum for long-lived Riesling and Gewurztraminer.

places.name: Bergheim
places.note: Village of Altenberg de Bergheim, a Grand Cru whose rules admit a blend of several grapes.

places.name: Kientzheim and Kaysersberg
places.note: Below the granite Schlossberg, the first site named Grand Cru in 1975, celebrated for Riesling.

places.name: Niedermorschwihr
places.note: Village of the steep granite Sommerberg, Riesling of tension and mineral drive.

places.name: Turckheim
places.note: Town of the granite Brand Grand Cru, Riesling and Pinot Gris of power.

places.name: Wintzenheim and Wettolsheim
places.note: Hengst, at Wintzenheim on marl and limestone, opened to Pinot Noir from the 2022 vintage; Wettolsheim beside it holds the Steingrubler Grand Cru.

places.name: Eguisheim
places.note: Village of the Eichberg and Pfersigberg Grand Crus and of a house known for resolutely dry wines.

places.name: Ammerschwihr
places.note: Kaefferkopf, the fifty-first Grand Cru added in 2007, which may be sold as a blend.

places.name: Rouffach
places.note: Vorbourg Grand Cru, with the walled Clos Saint Landelin inside it, admitted Pinot Noir in 2024; Côte de Rouffach is a communal name.

places.name: Guebwiller
places.note: Four Grand Crus on steep terraces, Kitterlé, Kessler, Saering and Spiegel, farmed by one large estate.

places.name: Thann
places.note: The southernmost and steepest Grand Cru, the volcanic Rangen, smoky Riesling and Pinot Gris.

producers.name: Trimbach

producers.name: Hugel & Fils

producers.name: Domaine Zind-Humbrecht
producers.why: Turckheim, biodynamic, with Grand Cru Brand and Rangen; rich and sometimes off-dry wines that put a sweetness scale on the label early.

producers.name: Domaine Weinbach
producers.why: Kaysersberg, below the Schlossberg, with a run of Rieslings from the granite.

producers.name: Domaine Marcel Deiss
producers.why: Bergheim, the champion of field blends by site, which the Altenberg de Bergheim rules now admit.

producers.name: Albert Boxler
producers.why: Niedermorschwihr grower on the Sommerberg and Brand granites.

producers.name: Domaine Ostertag
producers.why: Epfig in the Bas-Rhin, Muenchberg Riesling and Pinot Gris raised in barrels.

producers.name: Domaines Schlumberger
producers.why: Guebwiller, one of the largest estates in Alsace, with four Grand Crus on steep terraces.

producers.name: Léon Beyer

producers.name: Albert Mann

producers.name: Rolly Gassmann

producers.name: Domaine Schoffit

exam: Name the four noble grapes and the two late-harvest categories only they may carry.
Know that Alsace commonly names grapes: Riesling must be entirely Riesling, whereas Pinot Blanc may include Auxerrois.
Hold the count: 51 Grand Crus, each its own appellation since 2011, Schlossberg first in 1975.
Know Crémant d'Alsace's grapes, Pinot Blanc first, and that it is the second largest French sparkling appellation after Champagne.
Describe Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat by their tells and classic pairings.
Know Pinot Noir as the one black grape and its Grand Cru admission from the 2022 vintage.
Remember the 2021 sweetness-labelling rule and the flûte bottle.
traps: Pinot Blanc is important but not noble: no Grand Cru, no Vendanges Tardives.
Vendanges Tardives may finish nearly dry; Sélection de Grains Nobles is always sweet.
Check sweetness before recommending either Alsace Riesling or German Kabinett; neither name alone establishes the sweetness of every bottle.
Tokay d'Alsace was Pinot Gris; the name was retired by 2007 to protect Hungary's Tokaj.
Chardonnay is legal in Crémant d'Alsace and nowhere else in the appellation.
A Grand Cru that names no grape is a permitted blend, Altenberg de Bergheim or Kaefferkopf, not a mistake.
Edelzwicker and Gentil are both blends; Gentil is the stricter term.
Muscat here is dry; never promise a guest a sweet Muscat as in the Rhône or Roussillon.

cards.f: The four noble grapes of Alsace
cards.b: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat: the only grapes of Grand Cru, Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles, with a few site exceptions.

cards.f: Alsace Grand Cru: how many, and since when
cards.b: 51 named sites; the tier dates from 1975 (Schlossberg first), Kaefferkopf the last in 2007, each a separate appellation since 2011.

cards.f: Vendanges Tardives versus Sélection de Grains Nobles
cards.b: VT: late harvest at a set minimum sugar, may be dry or sweet. SGN: botrytised berries at a higher minimum, always sweet. Both noble grapes only, no chaptalisation.

cards.f: Crémant d'Alsace: grapes and the rosé rule
cards.b: Pinot Blanc leads, with Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Riesling and Chardonnay; rosé must be Pinot Noir alone. Traditional method.

cards.f: Tells of Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat in Alsace
cards.b: Riesling: citrus, acidity. Gewurztraminer: lychee, rose, lower acidity. Pinot Gris: smoky pear, weight. Muscat: grapey aromatics. Check sweetness on the label; aroma and grape alone do not establish residual sugar.

cards.f: Grand Cru exceptions to the noble-grape rule
cards.b: Sylvaner at Zotzenberg; blends at Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf; Pinot Noir at Hengst and Kirchberg de Barr (2022 vintage) and Vorbourg (2024).

cards.f: Alsace sweetness labelling rule since 2021
cards.b: AOC Alsace whites outside VT and SGN must indicate sec, demi-sec, moelleux or doux, either directly or on a clearly marked scale. Do not infer sweetness from the grape alone.

cards.f: Edelzwicker versus Gentil
cards.b: Edelzwicker: any blend of permitted whites, vintage optional. Gentil: at least 50 per cent noble grapes, each vinified separately.

questions.q: Which grape is one of Alsace's four noble varieties?
questions.exp: The noble four are Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat. Pinot Blanc, Sylvaner and Auxerrois make good everyday wine but, apart from Sylvaner at Zotzenberg, stay out of Grand Cru.

questions.q: How many Grand Cru sites does Alsace recognise?
questions.exp: Fifty-one named lieux-dits, each a separate appellation since 2011. Seventeen and forty-two are Champagne's Grand Cru and Premier Cru village counts; seven is the number of Chablis Grand Cru climats.

questions.q: What proportion of Riesling must an AOC Alsace wine labelled Riesling contain?
questions.exp: An AOC Alsace wine labelled Riesling must be entirely Riesling. Do not extend that answer to every grape name: Alsace Pinot Blanc may include Auxerrois, while Muscat can represent permitted Muscat varieties.

questions.q: Which Alsace label term names a botrytised wine that is always sweet?
questions.exp: Sélection de Grains Nobles is picked berry by berry from botrytised bunches at the highest minimum sugar. Vendanges Tardives may finish dry; Klevener is a grape mention and Crémant the sparkling wine.

questions.q: Which grape makes Crémant d'Alsace rosé?
questions.exp: The rosé must be Pinot Noir alone, the region's one black grape; the white Crémant leans on Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois, with Chardonnay allowed only in this appellation.

questions.q: Which Alsace Grand Cru admits Sylvaner under its own rules?
questions.exp: A 2005 amendment let Zotzenberg at Mittelbergheim write Sylvaner into its rules. Schlossberg (granite, the first Grand Cru), Rangen (volcanic, at Thann) and Brand (granite, Turckheim) keep to the noble four.

questions.q: From which vintage must a still Alsace white outside the late-harvest categories declare its sweetness on the label?
questions.exp: The 2021 rule applies to AOC Alsace white wines, except Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles. It requires sec, demi-sec, moelleux or doux, directly or on a clearly marked scale.

questions.q: Which is the one black grape permitted in AOC Alsace?
questions.exp: Pinot Noir is the one black grape of the appellation, making light reds, rosé and Crémant rosé, and since the 2022 vintage Grand Cru wine at Hengst and Kirchberg de Barr.

regions.name: Loire Valley
regions.summary: The Loire is France's longest river, and its wine region is a 400-kilometre corridor read from the Atlantic mouth upstream in four districts. The Pays Nantais makes Muscadet from Melon de Bourgogne; Anjou-Saumur is Chenin Blanc country, dry at Savennières and sweet on the Layon, with Cabernet Franc at Saumur-Champigny; Touraine holds Vouvray and Montlouis for Chenin in every style and Chinon and Bourgueil for Cabernet Franc; the Centre makes Sauvignon Blanc at Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé. Acidity runs through all of it, and the exam's first ask is which grape belongs to which name. Crémant de Loire is the traditional-method sparkling wine, and Pouilly-Fumé is never Pouilly-Fuissé.

terroir.climate: Maritime at Nantes, mild and damp with Atlantic frost in spring; increasingly continental upstream, so Sancerre has hard winters, hot summers and a real frost risk each April. Rain at harvest and rot are the autumn hazards, except on the Layon, where sheltering hills bring the misty mornings and dry afternoons that noble rot needs.
terroir.soils: Two basements meet near Saumur. To the west lies the old, hard Armorican rock, granite, gneiss, schist and gabbro, which gives Muscadet its salt and Savennières its austerity; to the east begins the soft Cretaceous limestone of the Paris Basin, the tuffeau, quarried for châteaux and cellars. The Centre adds Kimmeridgian marl (terres blanches), hard pebbly limestone (caillottes) and flint (silex), whose Sauvignon smells of struck match and gunsmoke.
terroir.topography: A broad, low valley with vines on gentle slopes and terraces above the floodplain, rarely higher than 300 metres. Tributaries carry the best sites: the Sèvre and Maine around Nantes, the Layon and Aubance in Anjou, the Cher, Indre and Vienne in Touraine. Sancerre is a steep hill town above the river, Pouilly its lower-lying neighbour on the opposite bank.
terroir.water: The Loire runs about 1,000 kilometres from the Massif Central to the Atlantic, and every district faces it or a tributary. The Sèvre and Maine name the best Muscadet; the Layon's mists make the sweet wines; the Cher, Indre, Vienne and Loir carry Touraine's appellations; Sancerre sits on the left bank, Pouilly-Fumé on the right.

grapes.name: Melon de Bourgogne
grapes.styles: Muscadet's only grape: neutral, bone dry, low in alcohol and saline, lifted by lees ageing.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: The great Loire white, fiercely acid and long-lived, dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling from Anjou to Touraine.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: The Centre's grape at Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé, Menetou-Salon, Quincy and Reuilly, and across Touraine: gooseberry, citrus, flint.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Breton locally: raspberry, pencil shavings and leaf at Chinon, Bourgueil, Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Red and rosé Sancerre and Menetou-Salon, and a share of the Centre's lighter reds.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: Light everyday Touraine red and the pale vin gris further upstream.

grapes.name: Grolleau
grapes.styles: The pink grape of off-dry Rosé d'Anjou.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: A small permitted share beside Cabernet Franc, and a partner in Cabernet d'Anjou rosé.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Called Côt here; a blending red in Touraine.

grapes.name: Pineau d'Aunis
grapes.styles: Peppery old red of the Loir valley, for pale rosé and light red.

grapes.name: Chasselas
grapes.styles: The grape of Pouilly-sur-Loire, the plain appellation on Pouilly-Fumé's ground.

grapes.name: Romorantin
grapes.styles: Cour-Cheverny's own grape, grown nowhere else of note.

wines.style: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie
wines.note: Dry, light, lemon and sea air with a yeasty prickle from a winter on its lees; the oyster wine.
Dry Chenin of great austerity and age: quince, beeswax and chalk; roast chicken or river fish.

wines.style: Coteaux du Layon, Quarts de Chaume, Bonnezeaux
wines.note: Botrytised Chenin, honey and apricot kept bright by acid; foie gras, blue cheese, fruit tarts.
Chenin in every style, sec, demi-sec, moelleux and sparkling; demi-sec with pork or spice, sec with river fish.
Cabernet Franc, light to medium, raspberry and pencil lead, often served cool; charcuterie, goat cheese, poultry.
The silkiest Loire Cabernet Franc, from tuffeau near Saumur, served slightly cool.
Sauvignon Blanc, citrus, gooseberry and flint, bone dry; Crottin de Chavignol goat cheese and shellfish.
Sauvignon from the right bank, smokier from flint, white only.
Pinot Noir, light and crunchy; the rosé is pale and dry.
Off-dry pinks, Grolleau in the first and the Cabernets in the second; Rosé de Loire is the dry one.
Traditional-method sparkling, Chenin-led with Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc, aged in the tuffeau caves around Saumur.

made.viticulture: Each district trains and picks to its own grape. Melon around Nantes grows on low Guyot vines over granite and gneiss, picked early to keep acidity high and alcohol low, with April frost off the Atlantic as the great hazard. Chenin is picked in several passes, tries, in Anjou and at Vouvray: a first for dry wine, later ones as the berries shrivel or take noble rot, so one slope can give sec, demi-sec and moelleux in a single autumn, and the grower decides only once the weather has shown its hand. Cryoextraction and chaptalisation are barred at Quarts de Chaume. Cabernet Franc in Touraine ripens on warm gravels and tuffeau slopes but must be picked fully ripe to avoid green pepper. Sauvignon in the Centre is wire-trained, machine-picked on flatter land and hand-picked on the steep Monts Damnés. Organic and biodynamic farming are widespread at Vouvray, Savennières, Montlouis and Sancerre.
made.winemaking: Muscadet's signature is sur lie: the wine stays on its fine lees through the winter without racking and is bottled straight off them from the March after harvest, taking a faint prickle of carbon dioxide and a yeasty roundness; the crus communaux go further, with around two years on the lees. Chenin ferments slowly, often in old demi-muids or neutral barrels, sometimes in steel; sweet wines stop on their own or by chilling and sulphur with the sugar they keep, and in the tuffeau caves they age for decades. Crémant de Loire and Vouvray mousseux and pétillant are traditional-method sparkling wines with a second fermentation in bottle; Montlouis's Pétillant Originel is bottled before the first fermentation ends, with no dosage. Cabernet Franc is destemmed, fermented at moderate temperatures and aged in old wood or concrete to keep its fruit. Sauvignon in the Centre is mostly steel and bottled early, though Chavignol's best sites see older oak, and the reds are light Pinot Noir with little new wood.

law.classification: The Loire follows the national ladder of Vin de France, IGP and AOC, with IGP Val de Loire (once Jardin de la France) covering the valley's country wine. The appellations are named for places and the grape is implied: Muscadet is Melon, Vouvray is Chenin, Sancerre white is Sauvignon, Chinon is Cabernet Franc. Rank above the village level is rare. Quarts de Chaume became the valley's first and only Grand Cru in 2011 and Chaume its only Premier Cru, within Coteaux du Layon; Savennières carries two named crus, Coulée de Serrant and Roche aux Moines; and Muscadet Sèvre et Maine had seven crus communaux in its rules by early 2026, the first three recognised in 2011, with longer lees ageing; La Haie-Fouassière, Vallet and Champtoceaux (in the Coteaux de la Loire) were put to public consultation in 2025. Sweetness words (sec, demi-sec, moelleux, doux) and sur lie are regulated terms, not house style. Crémant de Loire is the valley-wide traditional-method appellation.

Anjou, Saumur, Touraine, Muscadet: broad appellations across one district, red, white and rosé.
Village or communal AOC
Savennières, Vouvray, Chinon, Sancerre and the like: one place, one grape or two, the exam's core.

Premier Cru and Grand Cru

Dry to sweet; Vouvray and Montlouis use all of them
Fully sparkling and lightly sparkling Chenin by the traditional method

places.name: Pays Nantais
places.note: Around Nantes at the Atlantic mouth: Melon de Bourgogne on granite, gneiss, schist and gabbro, dry and saline, sur lie its signature.

places.name: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine
places.note: The largest and best Muscadet appellation, south-east of Nantes between its two rivers; home of sur lie and the crus communaux.

places.name: Crus communaux
places.note: Clisson, Gorges, Le Pallet, Goulaine, Château-Thébaud, Monnières-Saint-Fiacre and Mouzillon-Tillières, the seven in the rules by early 2026: village wines held around two years on their lees. La Haie-Fouassière, Vallet and Champtoceaux were put to consultation in 2025.

places.name: Muscadet Côtes de Grandlieu and Coteaux de la Loire
places.note: The two smaller Muscadet zones, by the lake south-west of Nantes and upstream towards Ancenis.

places.name: Gros Plant du Pays Nantais
places.note: Sharp, light white from Folle Blanche, the region's other grape.

places.name: Anjou-Saumur
places.note: Chenin Blanc on schist and then tuffeau around Angers and Saumur: dry Savennières, sweet Layon, the valley's rosés, Cabernet Franc at Saumur-Champigny and Saumur's sparkling cellars.

places.name: Savennières
places.note: Dry Chenin on dark schist on the north bank near Angers; two named crus inside it, Coulée de Serrant (a monopole) and Roche aux Moines.

places.name: Coteaux du Layon
places.note: Botrytised Chenin on the Layon's slopes, village names allowed on the label, Chaume as Premier Cru.

places.name: Quarts de Chaume
places.note: The Loire's only Grand Cru since 2011, a sheltered slope above Chaume; no chaptalisation, no cryoextraction.

places.name: Bonnezeaux
places.note: A second sweet Chenin appellation inside the Layon zone, on schist slopes.

places.name: Coteaux de l'Aubance
places.note: Sweet Chenin from the next valley north of the Layon, lighter in style.

places.name: Rochefort-sur-Loire
places.note: The village between Savennières and the Layon, with cellars making dry, sweet and Quarts de Chaume alike.

places.name: Anjou, Anjou-Villages, Rosé d'Anjou, Cabernet d'Anjou
places.note: The regional names: Chenin whites, Cabernet reds and off-dry pinks; Anjou-Villages Brissac is the stricter red.

places.name: Saumur
places.note: The town and regional appellation: Chenin whites, Cabernet reds, and tuffeau caves that age Crémant de Loire and Saumur mousseux.

places.name: Saumur-Champigny
places.note: Cabernet Franc on tuffeau south-east of Saumur, the valley's most polished red.

places.name: Saumur Puy-Notre-Dame and Coteaux de Saumur
places.note: A newer village red appellation and the sweet Chenin of the Saumur side.

places.name: Touraine
places.note: The middle Loire around Tours: Chenin at Vouvray and Montlouis, Cabernet Franc at Chinon and Bourgueil, Sauvignon and Gamay under the Touraine name.

places.name: Vouvray
places.note: Chenin on the north bank east of Tours, on tuffeau: sec, demi-sec, moelleux, mousseux and pétillant from the same slopes.

places.name: Montlouis-sur-Loire
places.note: Vouvray's mirror on the south bank, Chenin alone, with Pétillant Originel.

places.name: Chinon
places.note: Cabernet Franc on the Vienne, gravel for early drinking and tuffeau slopes for ageing, plus a little Chenin white.

places.name: Bourgueil
places.note: Cabernet Franc on the north bank, firmer and longer-lived than Chinon.

places.name: Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil
places.note: The lighter, sandier neighbour of Bourgueil, Cabernet Franc for early drinking.

places.name: Touraine AOC
places.note: Sauvignon Blanc white and Gamay red across the district, with communal names such as Chenonceaux.

places.name: Cheverny and Cour-Cheverny
places.note: Sauvignon-led whites and light reds near Blois; Cour-Cheverny is Romorantin alone.

places.name: Jasnières and Coteaux du Loir
places.note: On the river Loir to the north: Chenin whites at Jasnières, Pineau d'Aunis reds and rosés around it.

places.name: Valençay
places.note: Red, white and rosé at Touraine's eastern edge, sharing its name with a goat cheese.

places.name: Centre
places.note: The upper Loire around Sancerre: Sauvignon Blanc on limestone and flint, Pinot Noir for red and rosé, with Menetou-Salon, Quincy and Reuilly as the value ring.

places.name: Sancerre
places.note: The hill town on the left bank: Sauvignon on caillottes, terres blanches and silex; red and rosé from Pinot Noir.

places.name: Chavignol
places.note: The Sancerre village with the steep Monts Damnés on Kimmeridgian marl, and the Crottin goat cheese.

places.name: Pouilly-Fumé
places.note: Sauvignon on the right bank around Saint-Andelain, flint-smoked, white only.

places.name: Pouilly-sur-Loire
places.note: The same ground as Pouilly-Fumé, planted to Chasselas, plain and local.

places.name: Menetou-Salon
places.note: Sancerre's neighbour on the same Kimmeridgian marl: Sauvignon and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Quincy and Reuilly
places.note: Sauvignon on sand and gravel by the Cher and Arnon west of Bourges; Reuilly adds Pinot Gris rosé.

places.name: Coteaux du Giennois and Châteaumeillant
places.note: Outer Centre appellations: Sauvignon and light reds near Gien, Gamay vin gris to the south.

places.name: Orléans and Orléans-Cléry
places.note: Small appellations around Orléans, the latter for Cabernet Franc red.

places.name: Crémant de Loire
places.note: The valley-wide traditional-method sparkling appellation across Anjou, Saumur and Touraine, Chenin-led, centred on Saumur.

places.name: Val de Loire
places.note: IGP Val de Loire, the whole valley's country wine: varietal Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Gamay, grape on the label.

places.name: Upstream and outlying appellations
places.note: Fiefs Vendéens by the coast, Haut-Poitou, and Saint-Pourçain, Côte Roannaise, Côtes du Forez and Côtes d'Auvergne towards the source, Gamay and Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Domaine Huet
producers.why: Vouvray's benchmark since 1928, biodynamic, with three named sites, Le Haut-Lieu, Le Mont and Clos du Bourg, in every style from sec to moelleux and pétillant.

producers.name: Domaine du Clos Naudin
producers.why: Vouvray's other reference, dry and demi-sec wines of great length.

producers.name: Coulée de Serrant
producers.why: The Savennières monopole with its own appellation, planted by monks in the twelfth century and a cradle of biodynamics in France.

producers.name: Domaine des Baumard
producers.why: Rochefort-sur-Loire: Savennières, Coteaux du Layon and Quarts de Chaume from one cellar.

producers.name: Domaine de la Pépière
producers.why: Maisdon-sur-Sèvre grower whose cru communal Muscadets showed the region could age.

producers.name: Domaine de l'Ecu
producers.why: Le Landreau, biodynamic Muscadet bottled by soil: Granite, Gneiss and Orthogneiss.

producers.name: Clos Rougeard
producers.why: Saumur-Champigny's cult estate, Cabernet Franc raised in barrel, proof that Loire reds can age for decades.

producers.name: Domaine Vacheron
producers.why: Sancerre, biodynamic, serious Pinot Noir as well as Sauvignon.

producers.name: Didier Dagueneau
producers.why: Pouilly-Fumé's great modern estate at Saint-Andelain; Silex and Pur Sang set the standard for serious Sauvignon.

producers.name: Domaine de la Taille aux Loups
producers.why: Montlouis, dry Chenin and the Triple Zéro pétillant without chaptalisation, liqueur de tirage or dosage.

exam: Match grape to appellation: Muscadet Melon, Savennières and Vouvray Chenin, Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé Sauvignon, Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny Cabernet Franc.
Know sur lie and what it does to Muscadet.
Name the sweet Chenin zones and the Loire's only Grand Cru, Quarts de Chaume.
Know that Sancerre makes red and rosé from Pinot Noir and Pouilly-Fumé is white only.
Separate Pouilly-Fumé from Pouilly-Fuissé and from Pouilly-sur-Loire.
Know Crémant de Loire and the sparkling styles of Vouvray and Montlouis.
Place the four districts in order from the sea: Pays Nantais, Anjou-Saumur, Touraine, Centre.
Know the soil words: tuffeau, silex, caillottes, terres blanches.
traps: Pouilly-Fumé is Loire Sauvignon; Pouilly-Fuissé is Mâconnais Chardonnay; Pouilly-sur-Loire is Chasselas from Pouilly-Fumé's own ground.
Muscadet's grape is Melon de Bourgogne, not Muscat and not a grape called Muscadet.
Sancerre rouge is Pinot Noir, never Cabernet Franc.
Savennières is dry Chenin by custom and nearly always in the bottle; the sweet Layon wines are the same grape with the opposite intent.
Rosé d'Anjou and Cabernet d'Anjou are off-dry; Rosé de Loire is the dry one.
A Vouvray is not dry by default: read the label for sec, demi-sec or moelleux.
Fumé Blanc is a California name borrowed from Pouilly-Fumé, not a Loire appellation.
Chenin Blanc is also Steen in South Africa; the Loire never calls it that.

cards.f: Loire's four districts, mouth to source, with their lead grapes
cards.b: Pays Nantais (Melon de Bourgogne), Anjou-Saumur (Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc), Touraine (Chenin, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon), Centre (Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir).

cards.f: Sur lie: what it means
cards.b: The wine stays on its fine lees through the winter and is bottled straight off them from the March after harvest: a yeasty roundness and a faint prickle. Muscadet's signature.

cards.f: Sweet Chenin appellations of Anjou
cards.b: Coteaux du Layon (with Chaume as Premier Cru), Quarts de Chaume (Grand Cru, 2011), Bonnezeaux, Coteaux de l'Aubance: botrytised or shrivelled Chenin kept fresh by acid.

cards.f: Cabernet Franc appellations of the Loire
cards.b: Chinon, Bourgueil, Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil in Touraine; Saumur-Champigny in Anjou-Saumur. Light to medium, raspberry and pencil lead, served cool.

cards.f: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé: grapes and colours
cards.b: Both Sauvignon Blanc for white. Sancerre also makes red and rosé from Pinot Noir; Pouilly-Fumé is white only. Sancerre on the left bank, Pouilly on the right.

cards.f: The three Pouillys
cards.b: Pouilly-Fumé: Loire Sauvignon Blanc. Pouilly-sur-Loire: Chasselas on the same ground. Pouilly-Fuissé: Mâconnais Chardonnay in Burgundy.

cards.f: Vouvray's styles of Chenin
cards.b: All Chenin Blanc: sec, demi-sec, moelleux (sweet), and sparkling mousseux and pétillant by the traditional method. Montlouis across the river mirrors it.

cards.f: Soil words of the Loire
cards.b: Tuffeau: soft Cretaceous limestone of Touraine and Saumur. Silex: flint, Pouilly-Fumé's smoke. Caillottes: hard pebbly limestone at Sancerre. Terres blanches: Kimmeridgian marl.

cards.f: Rosé d'Anjou, Cabernet d'Anjou, Rosé de Loire
cards.b: Rosé d'Anjou: off-dry, Grolleau. Cabernet d'Anjou: off-dry to sweet, Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon. Rosé de Loire: dry.

questions.q: Which grape makes the wine called Muscadet?
questions.exp: Muscadet is Melon de Bourgogne alone, a neutral, acid grape brought from Burgundy. Folle Blanche makes the neighbouring Gros Plant; Chenin and Sauvignon belong further upstream.

questions.q: Which Loire appellation makes its red wine from Pinot Noir?
questions.exp: Sancerre's red and rosé are Pinot Noir. Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny are Cabernet Franc.

questions.q: Name the Loire's only Grand Cru appellation.
questions.exp: Quarts de Chaume, a sheltered slope above the Layon, was raised to Grand Cru in 2011; Chaume beside it is the valley's one Premier Cru. Both are sweet Chenin Blanc.

questions.q: Which Pouilly appellation is made from Sauvignon Blanc?
questions.exp: Pouilly-Fumé is Sauvignon from the right bank opposite Sancerre. Pouilly-Fuissé, Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles are Chardonnay appellations of the Mâconnais.

questions.q: What does sur lie mean on a Muscadet label?
accept: kept on its lees through the winter
questions.exp: The wine rests on its fine lees through the winter and is bottled directly off them from the following March, gaining texture and a slight prickle.

questions.q: Which grape makes the white wine Savennières?
questions.exp: Savennières is Chenin Blanc on schist on the Loire's north bank near Angers, dry and long-lived; Coulée de Serrant and Roche aux Moines are its named crus.

questions.q: Which grape makes the red wines of Chinon and Bourgueil?
questions.exp: Cabernet Franc, called Breton in Touraine, with a small share of Cabernet Sauvignon allowed: raspberry, pencil shavings and leaf, served slightly cool.

questions.q: Which of the Loire's four districts lies nearest the Atlantic?
questions.exp: The Pays Nantais, around Nantes at the river mouth, is the maritime district of Muscadet; Anjou-Saumur, Touraine and the Centre follow upstream in that order.
